# TEN DAYS OUT — Review Panel, Second Draft

Second draft read in full: 33,337 words (first draft: 32,261), 10 chapters. Same panel, same brief, same ground rules. Where a reviewer changed a verdict from the first draft, they say what in the text changed it.

---

## ROUND 1 — INDEPENDENT REVIEWS

### 1. THE KU READER — ★★★★☆ (4/5, up from 3.5)

**Verdict:** This is the version I'd finish, review well, and preorder Book 2 from — and the preorder is now easy, because I can see Book 2 standing at the end of this one.

**Three biggest strengths**
- **Beth's blind spot is now the best thing in the book.** In the first draft she solved the leak like a checklist. Now she *knows* at the bread rack in Ch.3 — "Tess knew I stayed" — and spends five days not knowing it: winding-clock memory, hands locked on the hatchet in Ch.6, defending her in bed in Ch.5 ("Tess has known where I sleep since I was nine"). That's how a person actually fails to see the person who raised her. I felt the Ch.8 wheelhouse scene — her laying the pieces out alone and saying "Tess" out loud to an empty room — in my stomach.
- **The third sex scene finally lands.** Moving it out of Ch.8 to Ch.10, in her own bed, in her own lit house, with the clock wound and nobody listening for anything — that's the first time the heat and the plot are the same event. "Somewhere in it she quit listening" is the whole book in one line. The mutual version of the rule — he reports the night before it's anywhere else; she previews her grand jury answer ("Yes… you can read the rest in the transcript") — made me trust the HEA.
- **The ending now sells the series.** Russ's hand coming off the piling at "three harbors" and closing on the envelope, Quist seasick and upright asking him to work the ledger with her — that's a Book 2 couple and a Book 2 case in one page. I'd buy it for them alone.

**Three biggest problems**
- **Heat is now an honest 3.5, still not 4.** Ch.5 and Ch.6 are unchanged — good scenes, short fuses. The front note now says "steamy, open-door," which matches what I got, so this is no longer a complaint about the book, only about the brief. If the listing promises more than "steamy," reviews will still dock it.
- **Ch.6 is still the chapter I skim.** It's the same length and the Tuesday ledger opening is still slow, though the kindling scene — her splitting sticks "too thin to hold a flame" because she will not say the emergency-management sentence — nearly saved the whole chapter for me.
- **She never tells Dane about Tess.** Five days of suspicion withheld from the man sleeping six feet away, and he takes a bullet graze in the middle of them. I accept the denial as psychology. As a reader who loved this heroine *because she never does the stupid thing*, this is the closest she comes, and the book never has Dane say so.

**Where I'd have stopped:** Nowhere. Skimmed the Ch.6 ledger pages only.
**Change first:** One line in Ch.8 where Dane names the withholding and she owns it. The reconciliation scene can carry it; right now it lets her off a hook it put her on.

---

### 2. THE DEVELOPMENTAL EDITOR — ★★★★☆ (4/5, up from 3.5)

**Verdict:** The revision did the hardest thing a revision can do: it didn't just fix the named problems, it converted the book's biggest structural liability — a leak the reader solves at 55% — into its central character arc.

**On the leak, revisited:** My first-draft note stands for the reader (margin: Ch.3; certainty: Ch.6, the emergency-management line). What changed is what the book *does* with it. Beth now clocks the same clue the reader does, on the same schedule — bread rack Ch.3, hatchet Ch.6 ("Local emergency management on Cutter wore a red vest… She didn't say it") — and the suspense of the second half is no longer whodunit but *when will she let herself know*. Ch.7 even gives her the mechanism in plain sight: "If it was him, it wasn't her." That is a fair mystery and a fair character study running on the same evidence. This is the correct answer to "too early."

**Three biggest strengths**
- **Tess is reconciled.** The $9,000 now has a chain: Arsenault at the back door at 6:15 Friday morning, the envelope, "a paid witness is a witness nobody believes" — supplied *to* her, planted *by* her, inside a story she believed for four days ("Scare you off before the grand jury, nobody hurt"), and exited on Thursday noon at the price of a threat against the *North Reach* with Ned asleep aboard. The frame-up is now the same crime as the leaking — doing what Arsenault told her inside a lie about its purpose — and the ending's coldness is calibrated to it: Beth doesn't cross the brow, the saltines go into a pocket instead of a hand, Ned's hands stay in his pockets.
- **The reconciliation is earned on the page.** She opens the notebook herself, puts her own finger under *not disclosed*, makes him answer for the struck-through line, and sets a condition with a price ("Nothing about me goes in that book or up that phone that I haven't heard first" — and he accepts being called a coach by his own supervisor). No sex that day. The Ch.10 night scene then pays the condition off in both directions.
- **Continuity repairs I flagged are made.** Russ's arrest is now physically explained (cellar bulkhead, stair behind the desk, Arsenault calling the skiff back with his hands on the radio); the indictment is split — Pelletier voted Monday, the second returned Tuesday — which is how it would actually happen; the trap plan now pre-agrees Beth's descent to the deck, so Ch.9 runs on a decision instead of an improvisation.

**Three biggest problems**
- **Ch.6 was enriched, not rebuilt.** Same length (3,341 words vs 3,308). Every day now carries a leak-beat, so the sag is purposeful — but it remains the slowest chapter, and a cold reader who doesn't know the Tess arc is the point may still feel three days of errands. This is now a judgement call, not a defect.
- **The trigger for Beth's Ch.3 knowledge is under-written.** "Tess knew I stayed" arrives whole, off a conversation about a cell booster. I believe her body knows; I am less sure a first-time reader will be able to say *what* she knows at that moment, which matters because the next five days hang on it. Two sentences of specific content — what Tess said in the check-in call that only a woman passing it on would repeat — would lock it.
- **The withholding is never adjudicated.** Beth keeps a material suspicion from her protector through an armed ambush. The book treats it as denial; an unsympathetic reader can treat it as the brief's forbidden stupid choice. Dane, of all people, would name it. That he doesn't reads as the book protecting its heroine.

**Change first:** The Ch.8 adjudication beat the KU Reader also wants — one exchange, not a scene. Everything else I asked for last time is in the text.

---

### 3. THE LINE EDITOR / AI-PROSE SPOTTER — ★★★½ (3.5/5, up from 3)

**Verdict:** The de-regularisation pass is real, measurable, and incomplete — it reads like a book that has been edited by someone who was given my first report as a checklist, which I mean as a compliment with a warning attached.

**What measurably changed** (first draft → second draft, my own counts)
- "Put it where she put the things…" — 3 → **0**. "Counted" — 19 → **7**. "Didn't ask" — 14 → **3**. Objects "squared" — 9 → **4**. "Burnt coffee and wet wool" wheelhouse — 3 → **1**. Ned's hearing aid — 7 mentions → **2**. The 340 steps — 3 recurrences → **1**. The Ch.4 generator scene has lost its stroke-counting entirely; the primer now just runs "until the fuel ran clean."
- Average sentence length 10.7 → 11.6 words; short fragments 22.1% → 20.5% of sentences. Subtle, but the metronome is audibly looser.
- **Dane now thinks in a different syntax than Beth.** His POV passages (Ch.2 slip, Ch.8 ledge, Ch.9 eleven o'clock, Ch.10 rail) run longer, subordinated, retrospective — "and he supposed he would be doing that for the rest of his life" is a sentence Beth's narration would never produce. Beth remains clipped and inventory-driven. The first draft's single-register problem is roughly half fixed: narration yes, dialogue not yet — in conversation they still trade the same aphoristic short lines.

**What remains**
- The scene-ending cadence survives: withheld action, short final line ("She didn't step out" is still there, Ch.2). Fragments are still one sentence in five.
- "Hands" is still the book's master image (63 instances) — now mostly earned, since the plot literally runs on whose hands were on what, but a spotter will still find the density machine-high.
- The tell has moved up a level: the *revisions themselves* are suspiciously systematic. Every tic I named was reduced, none was over-corrected, and the fixes distribute evenly across chapters. Human revision is messier and more local. A hostile spotter will now say "AI draft, AI line edit against a human-supplied report" — which happens to be true, and is harder to distinguish from a diligent human edit than anything in the first draft was.

**Do the leads sound like different people?** In narration, now yes, mostly. At the kitchen table, not quite.
**Change first:** A dialogue-only pass — give Dane back the Lowell rhythms his backstory promises and let Beth be the only one who talks like a logbook.

### 4. THE KDP MARKET STRATEGIST — ★★★½ (3.5/5, unchanged, for now)

**Verdict:** The text is now publishable-grade for this category; the product around it still doesn't exist, and my rating is for the product.

**What improved commercially**
- **The series engine is visible.** First draft: a hook I couldn't parse. Second draft: Quist + Russ + a three-harbor ledger case + "work it with me this winter." That's a Book 2 with a built-in couple, a built-in case, and a first scene already written. Series read-through is the entire economics of a 33k-word book, and this draft finally loads that gun.
- **The front note now tells the truth** — "steamy, open-door" — which is what the text delivers. If the blurb adopts the same two words, the expectation mismatch I flagged as the largest commercial risk is closed. Note "if": no cover, title treatment, subtitle or blurb was in the file, so the brief's "PG-13 packaging" question remains *untested*, not resolved.
- **Length economics unchanged:** 33,337 words, roughly the same KU page count and the same sub-dollar full read as before. $2.99 in KU, Book 2 on preorder at launch, ads only against series value — that plan is unaltered, but it's now a plan for a series that demonstrably has a second book in it.

**Remaining problems**
- **[PEN NAME] is still on the title page** and there is still no packaging in evidence. A manuscript can now survive review; a listing still can't be built from this file.
- **The withholding beat is a review-risk.** A slice of this genre's readership polices heroine competence hard (it was in the brief for a reason). Expect some "she hid it for five days??" three-stars. The denial framing will save it with most readers; it won't save it with all.
- **Russ/Quist as Book 2 leads is an asset with a clock on it.** If Book 2 isn't Russ's book, the epilogue over-promises. Lock the series order before launch, not after.

**Change first:** Same as last time, now cheaper: don't launch alone — but the difference is that "alone" is now a scheduling decision, not a writing problem.

---

### 5. THE SKEPTIC — ★★★☆ (3/5, up from 2.5/3 after cross-talk last round)

**Verdict:** My strongest first-draft charge — that everyone in this book is a mechanism — no longer survives Ch.3 to Ch.8, and I'll say so plainly. What survives is narrower and, for a publisher, harder.

**What I concede**
- Beth's self-deception is not a mechanism. A mechanism would have solved the mystery; this woman *declines* to, at cost, for reasons the book shows instead of stating — a clock wound the night her father died, soup carried up a hill. The line "If it was him, it wasn't her" is the most human sentence in either draft, because it's an ugly piece of reasoning a real person would be ashamed of later. The pipeline produced that. I didn't think it could.
- Tess's arc is now a person making worsening choices inside a story she was told, which is what actual collaboration looks like.

**What stands**
- **The engineering is still total.** Every plant still pays: bulkhead, binder, brow chain, float timer, the box of condoms bought in Ch.6 opened in Ch.10 with "he took one from Tess's box." Real life, and real first novels, have slack. This has none, and some readers will still feel handled — they'll just be a smaller minority than for the first draft.
- **The spotability problem moved, it didn't die.** See the Line Editor: the fix pattern is legible as a process. If a "how this book was made" thread appears post-launch, the receipts are in the text's own revision geometry.
- **Nothing in this draft answers the disclosure question.** KDP's AI-generated-content disclosure at upload, and the pen name's public stance, are still decisions the humans haven't visibly made. The book got better; the risk I care most about is untouched by definition, because it was never in the text.

**Change first:** Same as before — decide what the pen name says about how this was made, before launch, in writing. The text has now done everything the text can do.

## ROUND 2 — CROSS-TALK

**Disagreement 1 — Does Beth's withholding break the brief?**
The Editor presses it: "The brief's first design goal was a heroine who never makes a stupid choice in danger. Withholding a suspect from your protector for five days is the genre's canonical stupid choice, re-dressed." The KU Reader disagrees on the reading experience: "She never gives Tess anything new after Saturday — no location, no plan. The leaks run through Ned and the emergency-management channel, not through her mouth. She starved the channel while lying to herself about why. That's denial, not a TSTL beat, and the distinction is the book now."
Editor's response, and the panel's nearest thing to a ruling: both readings are available in the text, and the book chooses neither — one adjudicating exchange in Ch.8 would choose the first. **No rating changes on this point; it becomes the Chair's first fix.**

**Disagreement 2 — Is Ch.6 fixed?**
Line Editor: "By content, yes — the kindling scene is the chapter's new centre. By shape, no — identical length." Strategist: "KU readers don't measure chapters; they measure whether they put the book down. I think fewer do now."
**Strategist changes his rating: 3.5 → 4.** "Not for Ch.6. Because the Russ/Quist epilogue converts my 'series funnel' argument from a plan into an observable fact of the text. My remaining objections are packaging, and packaging is no longer this manuscript's fault."

**Disagreement 3 — Did the line pass fool anyone?**
Skeptic: "It fooled the checklist. It wouldn't fool a motivated reader with both drafts." Line Editor: "No reader will have both drafts. Judge the artefact they'd actually meet." Skeptic: "Fair. Against the artefact alone, my generic objection is down to the payoff density."
**Skeptic changes his rating: 3 → 3.5.** "The denial arc is character work I said this pipeline couldn't do. I'm revising the claim, not the caution — the disclosure issue is a launch decision and it still hasn't been made."

KU Reader and Developmental Editor hold at 4. Line Editor holds at 3.5.

---

## ROUND 3 — CHAIR'S SYNTHESIS

**Consensus rating: 3.8/5** (KU Reader 4, Developmental Editor 4, Line Editor 3.5, Strategist 4, Skeptic 3.5) — up from 3.3/5 on the first draft.

**Verdict:** The second draft fixes four of the five changes this panel ranked last time, and the one it only half-fixes (Ch.6) it improves by content rather than by cutting. Tess's motive chain is complete, the reconciliation is earned and visibly priced, the series hook is legible, the arrest and the indictments now obey physics and procedure, and the prose has been measurably de-regularised. What remains is one unadjudicated moral beat, one slow chapter, a handful of one-line continuity slips, and every launch decision the first panel named — none of which is a structural problem any more.

**Scorecard against the panel's first-draft five**
1. *Reconcile Tess* — **Done.** Supplier, story she believed, exit attempt, threat, confession all cohere.
2. *Earn the Ch.8 reconciliation* — **Done.** On-page verification, a stated condition, a cost to Dane, and the third scene relocated to Ch.10 where it functions as restoration rather than reward.
3. *Rebuild Ch.6* — **Half-done.** Each day now advances the leak; the chapter is the same length and still the slowest.
4. *Clarify the Russ hook* — **Done.** An explicit recruitment, a refusal that is really an acceptance, and a Book 2 couple seeded.
5. *Settle the heat contract* — **Done in the text** ("steamy, open-door," third scene deepened). **Open in the listing** — no cover or blurb exists in the file to judge.

**The five remaining changes, ranked (all small)**
1. **Adjudicate the withholding.** One Ch.8 exchange in which Dane names Beth's five days of silence about Tess and she owns the reason. (Editor, KU Reader)
2. **Give Beth's Ch.3 knowledge a specific trigger** — one concrete thing Tess says or writes that Beth's body files before her mind does. (Editor)
3. **Compress Ch.6 by ~10%** — the Tuesday ledger opening is the only remaining passage two reviewers still skim. (KU Reader, Line Editor)
4. **Pay off or cut the boot-print photograph (Ch.3).** One line in Ch.10 — Quist matching it to Doucette's boots — closes the last dropped thread. (Editor, Chair)
5. **Dialogue voice pass for Dane** — the narration now differs from Beth's; the speech doesn't yet. (Line Editor)

**Continuity and logic — checked**
- *Fixed since draft 1:* Russ's arrest mechanics; the indictment timeline; the trap-plan pre-agreement; the store confession's money chain (Arsenault's 6:15am Friday visit precedes the Friday bank bag, so the deposit timeline now closes).
- *Still open from draft 1:* (a) The ferry deadheads back to Cutter Thursday night (Ch.1) yet Dane arrives on the "eight o'clock out of Pruett" (Ch.2) — the boat's overnight position still flips, and it is now the most visible slip in the book precisely because everything else was repaired. One sentence fixes it. (b) Ned calling the district from the store, "the only phone on the island now" (Ch.3), against Beth's dead line the same morning — still unexplained; one clause (the booster phone) fixes it.
- *New in this draft:* the watch alarm. Ch.7 sets it for "quarter past eleven"; Ch.8's Dane remembers setting it "at eleven" — a fifteen-minute discrepancy introduced by the revision, in a book that elsewhere keeps time to the minute.
- *Re-cleared:* Calendar (Thu Nov 12 – Mon Nov 23), injury side and restrictions, gait/heel logic, condom progression, barometer — all still exact.

**Publishable?** **Publishable after a light pass — a day's work, not another draft.** The remaining text fixes are items 1–5 above plus the three one-line continuity repairs; none requires a new scene longer than a paragraph. Before KDP, a human must still: replace [PEN NAME]; commission the cover/blurb to the "steamy, open-door" position the text now takes and abandon the brief's PG-13 instruction in writing; make the KDP AI-generated-content disclosure and settle the pen name's public stance *before* launch; and lock Book 2 as Russ/Quist with a preorder live on day one, because the epilogue now promises exactly that book.

**On the experiment:** The most informative thing about this draft is *which* fixes the pipeline could make. Given specific, located criticism, it executed all of it — including the sophisticated kind: relocating a sex scene to change its meaning, converting a plot hole (an early-solved leak) into a character arc, and repairing procedure. Its revisions are weakest exactly where its drafting was: it enriched Ch.6 instead of cutting it, because generating is easier for this system than deleting, and it introduced a fresh fifteen-minute error while repairing older ones, because no agent in the chain is reading cold. The updated conclusion: the pipeline plus one round of specific human-panel criticism produces a manuscript at the level of a competent human author's second draft. The remaining gap to a publishable book is no longer writing quality — it is judgement calls the pipeline cannot make for itself (what to cut, what to disclose, how to package), and one bible-blind cold read, which this panel is still not, and the next test still needs.
